careerCategories.name: Reactor Operations & Power Engineering
careerCategories.description: Careers that keep nuclear power stations and research reactors running safely — operating controls, maintaining equipment, and designing plant systems.

careerCategories.name: Radiopharmaceutical & Nuclear Medicine Sciences
careerCategories.description: Careers that produce, handle, and use radioactive materials for medical diagnosis and treatment, from lab-based radiochemistry to hospital imaging and radiopharmacy.

careerCategories.name: Regulatory & Radiation Safety
careerCategories.description: Careers focused on protecting people and the environment from radiation risk, from hospital and plant health-physics roles to industrial inspection.

careerCategories.name: Quality & Regulatory Affairs
careerCategories.description: Careers that keep isotope and radiopharmaceutical production compliant and safe to release, from lab-based quality control to licensing and GMP quality systems.

careerCategories.name: Research & Clinical Support
careerCategories.description: Careers that develop new radiopharmaceuticals and support their use in patient care, from preclinical research through clinical trials, dosimetry, and medical affairs.

careerCategories.name: Commercial, Logistics & Program Operations
careerCategories.description: Careers that get isotope products, projects, and partnerships across the finish line, from time-critical radioactive-material logistics to sales and program management.

careers.title: Nuclear Reactor Operator (Power Engineer)
careers.summary: Runs and monitors the control-room equipment that keeps a nuclear power station generating electricity safely.
careers.description: Nuclear reactor operators are power engineers who work in the control rooms of nuclear generating stations, running and monitoring reactors, turbines, boilers, and auxiliary equipment. They watch instruments and alarms for signs of malfunction, adjust plant systems to keep operations within safe limits, and log everything that happens on shift. Control room operators must be licensed by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC), and Ontario power engineers work their way up through provincial certification classes as they gain experience.
responsibilities: Operate automated and computerized control systems for reactors, turbines, boilers, and generators
Start up and shut down plant equipment and regulate transmission loads and voltages
Monitor instruments, gauges, and alarms to detect leaks or malfunctions
Record instrument readings and log operation, maintenance, and safety activities
Respond to abnormal conditions and coordinate with other plant systems operators
Assist in developing operating, maintenance, and safety procedures
careers.dayToDay: Most of the shift is spent in a control room watching screens and gauges, making small adjustments, and responding quickly if something drifts outside its normal range.

careers.title: Health / Radiation Physicist
careers.summary: Studies and manages radiation exposure to keep workers, patients, and the public safe in hospitals, nuclear plants, and research labs.
careers.description: Health and medical physicists apply the physics of radiation to protect people. In hospitals they work alongside radiation oncologists on cancer-treatment planning and equipment safety; in the nuclear industry they monitor and model radiation levels around plants and fuel-handling operations. The role falls under Canada's broader 'Physicists and astronomers' occupational group, and growth in nuclear power investment plus oncology and nuclear-medicine departments is expected to create more demand for health-physics specialists specifically.
responsibilities: Measure and model radiation levels and doses in clinical or industrial settings
Calibrate and test radiation-producing and radiation-detecting equipment
Develop radiation-safety procedures and threat-detection protocols
Support cancer treatment planning alongside radiation oncologists
Investigate and report on abnormal radiation readings or exposures
Advise on shielding, containment, and emergency-response design
careers.dayToDay: Work mixes hands-on equipment checks and dose calculations with writing safety reports, and some roles (especially in hospitals) involve regular contact with clinical treatment teams.

careers.title: Radiochemist / Nuclear Chemistry Technologist
careers.summary: Analyzes and handles radioactive materials and compounds, supporting everything from radiopharmaceutical production to nuclear plant water chemistry.
careers.description: Chemists in the isotope industry — sometimes called radiochemists or nuclear lab technologists depending on the employer — conduct research and quality-control analysis involving radioactive and non-radioactive compounds. They work in university and government research labs, radiopharmaceutical manufacturers, and nuclear generating stations, where they monitor coolant and fuel chemistry and support radioactive-materials handling. A bachelor's degree is the typical entry point, with a master's or doctorate usually required for research-chemist roles; licensing is voluntary in Ontario.
responsibilities: Analyze, synthesize, purify, and characterize chemical and radiochemical compounds
Run quality-control programs on raw materials, intermediates, and final radiopharmaceutical products
Conduct research into new chemical and radiochemical processes
Monitor and report on nuclear plant or lab water and materials chemistry
Maintain radiation-safety and containment procedures in the lab
Supervise chemical or nuclear lab technicians and technologists
careers.dayToDay: Days are spent largely at the bench or in an instrumentation lab running tests and interpreting results, balanced with documentation to satisfy safety and regulatory requirements.

careers.title: Nuclear Medicine Technologist
careers.summary: Prepares and administers radioactive tracers and operates imaging cameras to help diagnose disease in hospital patients.
careers.description: Nuclear medicine technologists are medical radiation technologists who prepare radiopharmaceuticals, inject tracers into patients, and operate gamma cameras, SPECT/CT, and PET/CT scanners to produce diagnostic images. The images show how organs and tissues are functioning at a cellular level, which helps doctors diagnose and plan treatment for cancer and other diseases. Registration with the College of Medical Radiation and Imaging Technologists of Ontario (CMRITO) is required to practise in the province.
responsibilities: Prepare and safely handle radioactive tracers and radiopharmaceuticals
Administer tracers to patients and monitor them during the procedure
Operate gamma cameras, SPECT/CT, and related imaging equipment
Follow radiation-safety precautions to protect patients, themselves, and colleagues
Process and quality-check diagnostic images for the interpreting physician
Maintain patient records and equipment calibration logs
careers.dayToDay: The role is patient-facing and hands-on: explaining the procedure, injecting tracers, positioning patients at the scanner, and keeping to a tight imaging schedule.

careers.title: Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) Technician
careers.summary: Uses X-ray, ultrasonic, and other techniques to check welds, pipes, and structures for hidden flaws without damaging them.
careers.description: Non-destructive testers and inspectors examine manufactured parts and structures — from pipelines to aircraft to nuclear plant components — for cracks or defects using radiographic, ultrasonic, magnetic-particle, liquid-penetrant, and eddy-current methods. Industrial radiographers who use a radioactive isotope source must pass a CNSC exam to become a certified exposure-device operator. Certification through Natural Resources Canada is available in three levels and is usually required by employers, and welding-inspector certification through the Canadian Welding Bureau is common as well.
responsibilities: Set up, calibrate, and operate radiographic, ultrasonic, and other NDT equipment
Conduct tests to detect discontinuities or defects in materials and welds
Interpret radiographs, digital readouts, and other test results
Follow radiation-safety rules when using isotope-based radiographic sources
Document findings in inspection and compliance reports
Advise on repair, rejection, or further testing of inspected components
careers.dayToDay: Work is often on-site at a plant, pipeline, or fabrication shop, moving between test locations and combining physical inspection work with report writing.

careers.title: Nuclear Engineer
careers.summary: Designs, analyzes, and improves the systems that make nuclear reactors and fuel cycles work safely and efficiently.
careers.description: Nuclear engineers are classified within Canada's broader Mechanical engineers occupational group. They research, design, and develop the reactors, fuel-handling systems, and safety systems used in nuclear power generation, and can also work on non-power applications of nuclear technology such as isotope production. Nuclear engineers are employed by utilities, engineering consulting firms, national laboratories, and equipment manufacturers, and typically hold a bachelor's degree in nuclear or mechanical engineering plus professional engineering (P.Eng.) licensure for senior roles.
responsibilities: Design and analyze reactor cores, fuel systems, and plant safety systems
Model reactor physics, heat transport, and thermal-hydraulic performance
Evaluate and improve the operation and maintenance of nuclear plant equipment
Support licensing submissions and regulatory compliance work with the CNSC
Investigate non-power applications of nuclear technology, including isotope production
Collaborate with operations, health-physics, and waste-management teams
careers.dayToDay: Most work happens at a desk doing engineering analysis, modelling, and documentation, punctuated by site visits, design reviews, and meetings with operations and regulatory staff.

careers.title: Radiopharmacist
careers.summary: A hospital or industrial pharmacist specialized in compounding, quality-testing, and dispensing radioactive drugs used in nuclear medicine.
careers.description: Radiopharmacists are pharmacists (Canada's Pharmacists occupational group) who focus on radiopharmaceuticals: drugs that contain a radioactive isotope, used to diagnose and treat disease in nuclear medicine departments. They compound and quality-test these products under strict radiation-safety rules, dispense them to nuclear medicine technologists, and advise clinical staff on dosing, handling, and interactions. The role requires a pharmacy degree and pharmacist licensure, plus additional specialized training and often certification in nuclear pharmacy.
responsibilities: Compound and quality-test radiopharmaceutical products before release
Calculate and verify radioactive doses for individual patients
Maintain radiation-safety, shielding, and waste-handling procedures in the pharmacy
Advise physicians and technologists on radiopharmaceutical selection and interactions
Maintain regulatory records for radioactive material use and inventory
Participate in research on new radiopharmaceutical products and protocols
careers.dayToDay: Work centres on a shielded compounding lab, preparing and checking doses against strict deadlines tied to each isotope's short half-life, alongside regulatory paperwork and consults with clinical teams.

careers.title: Nuclear Reactor Analyst / Reactor Physicist
careers.summary: Uses physics and computer modelling to calculate how neutrons and radiation behave inside a reactor so isotopes and power are produced safely and efficiently.
careers.description: Nuclear reactor analysts and reactor physicists model neutron flux, radiation transport, and reactor core behaviour to support isotope irradiation planning, reactor licensing, and safety cases. They work closely with reactor operators and engineers at research and power reactors to plan irradiation experiments, verify shielding, and interpret detector data. The role blends advanced physics with hands-on collaboration in a licensed nuclear facility.
responsibilities: Model neutron and radiation transport using simulation software to predict reactor and irradiation behaviour
Plan and evaluate target placement and irradiation schedules for isotope production runs
Analyze reactor physics data and detector readings to verify safety margins
Support licensing submissions and safety analysis reports for regulators
Collaborate with reactor operators, engineers, and radiochemists on experiment design
Document methods and findings for internal review and regulatory audits
careers.dayToDay: A typical day involves running or reviewing reactor physics simulations, meeting with operations staff to plan an upcoming irradiation cycle, and analyzing data from a previous run to confirm isotope yields matched predictions.

careers.title: Isotope Production Technician / Nuclear Technologist
careers.summary: Prepares irradiation targets and processes them afterward to recover, package, and ship medical isotopes safely.
careers.description: Isotope production technicians and nuclear technologists handle the hands-on work of turning an irradiated target into a usable isotope product. They prepare and load targets, operate hot cells and processing equipment to chemically recover isotopes, run quality checks, and package material for shipment to radiopharmacies and hospitals under strict radiation-safety procedures. The work requires precision, comfort working with radioactive material, and close attention to regulatory documentation.
responsibilities: Prepare and load irradiation targets according to production schedules
Operate hot cells, shielded processing equipment, and remote handling tools to recover isotopes
Perform in-process quality checks on isotope purity and activity levels
Package and label radioactive material for shipment following transport regulations
Maintain radiation dose logs and equipment maintenance records
Follow radiation protection and contamination control procedures at all times
careers.dayToDay: A shift typically includes loading or unloading targets from a hot cell, running chemical separation steps to recover the isotope, and completing documentation and dose logs before releasing product for shipment.

careers.title: Cyclotron Operator / Accelerator Technologist
careers.summary: Runs and maintains the particle accelerator that bombards targets with protons to make PET and other medical isotopes.
careers.description: Cyclotron operators and accelerator technologists start up, monitor, and shut down cyclotrons used to produce medical isotopes such as those used in PET imaging. They troubleshoot beam and vacuum systems, perform preventive maintenance on high-voltage and mechanical components, and work with radiochemistry teams to coordinate irradiation runs. The job combines electromechanical trade skills with radiation-safety discipline in a highly regulated production environment.
responsibilities: Start up, tune, and monitor cyclotron beam parameters during production runs
Perform preventive and corrective maintenance on accelerator, vacuum, and cooling systems
Coordinate target irradiation schedules with production and chemistry teams
Troubleshoot mechanical, electrical, and radio-frequency system faults
Maintain radiation safety interlocks and complete equipment logbooks
Support installation and commissioning of new accelerator components
careers.dayToDay: A typical day includes pre-run system checks, operating the cyclotron console during target bombardment, and performing scheduled maintenance or troubleshooting between production runs.
topEmployers: Centre for Probe Development and Commercialization (CPDC)

careers.title: Radiopharmaceutical / Production Technologist
careers.summary: Compounds, tests, and packages radioactive drugs in a manufacturing or hospital lab so they are safe and ready to ship.
careers.description: Radiopharmaceutical production technologists prepare, compound, and package radioactive drug products in licensed manufacturing or hospital radiopharmacy settings, working under pharmacists and production supervisors. They follow strict aseptic and Good Manufacturing Practice procedures, perform in-process checks, and manage inventory and documentation for products with short shelf lives. Because radiopharmaceuticals decay quickly, timing, accuracy, and radiation safety are central to the job.
responsibilities: Compound and prepare radiopharmaceutical doses following validated production procedures
Perform aseptic technique and in-process quality checks during manufacturing
Package, label, and stage products for time-sensitive shipment
Maintain batch records, inventory, and controlled-substance documentation
Support cleaning, calibration, and maintenance of production equipment
Follow radiation protection procedures and monitor personal dose
careers.dayToDay: A typical day is built around production schedules tied to isotope decay, with technologists compounding batches, running quality checks, and packaging doses in time for same-day courier pickup.

careers.title: Quality Control Analyst / QC Chemist
careers.summary: Tests radiopharmaceutical products in the lab to confirm they are pure, correctly identified, and safe to release.
careers.description: Quality control analysts and QC chemists run laboratory tests, such as chromatography, radiochemical purity testing, and sterility checks, to confirm that isotopes and radiopharmaceuticals meet release specifications before they leave the facility. They document results against Good Manufacturing Practice standards, investigate out-of-specification results, and support product release decisions. The role requires strong analytical chemistry skills and comfort working with radioactive samples.
responsibilities: Perform analytical tests such as chromatography, radiochemical purity, and endotoxin testing
Compare test results against product release specifications
Document and investigate out-of-specification or atypical results
Calibrate and maintain laboratory instruments
Prepare certificates of analysis and QC records for batch release
Support audits and regulatory inspections with accurate testing records
careers.dayToDay: A typical day involves running scheduled assays on production samples, reviewing chromatography or counting data against specifications, and documenting results in time to support same-day product release.

careers.title: Quality Assurance Specialist
careers.summary: Keeps the quality system running so a facility making radioactive products consistently meets regulatory and safety standards.
careers.description: Quality assurance specialists build and maintain the quality management systems that let isotope and radiopharmaceutical manufacturers meet Good Manufacturing Practice and regulatory requirements. They manage deviations, corrective and preventive actions (CAPA), change control, and internal audits, and act as a key contact during regulatory inspections. The role sits at the intersection of science, documentation, and process improvement.
responsibilities: Maintain and improve quality management system documentation and procedures
Investigate deviations and manage corrective and preventive action (CAPA) plans
Review batch records and manage change control processes
Plan and conduct internal audits and support external regulatory inspections
Coordinate training on quality procedures across production teams
Track quality metrics and report trends to management
careers.dayToDay: A typical day includes reviewing batch documentation for completeness, following up on open deviations or CAPAs, and meeting with production and QC teams to resolve quality issues before the next release.

careers.title: Radiation Safety Officer / Radiation Safety Specialist
careers.summary: Protects workers, the public, and the environment by monitoring radiation levels and enforcing safety rules at a nuclear or radiopharma facility.
careers.description: Radiation safety officers run the day-to-day radiation protection program at licensed nuclear and radiopharmaceutical facilities, applying the ALARA (as low as reasonably achievable) principle to keep doses down. They monitor radiation levels, manage personal dosimetry programs, investigate incidents, and act as the facility's main point of contact with the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC) for licensing and compliance matters. Certification by the CNSC is typically required to hold this role.
responsibilities: Monitor radiation levels and contamination using survey instruments
Manage personal dosimetry programs and review worker dose records
Investigate radiation safety incidents and implement corrective actions
Maintain the facility's Radiation Protection Program and related procedures
Act as primary contact with the CNSC for licensing and compliance
Deliver radiation safety training to staff
careers.dayToDay: A typical day includes conducting radiation surveys around production and storage areas, reviewing dosimetry reports, and following up on any readings or procedural questions raised by staff.

careers.title: Regulatory Affairs Specialist
careers.summary: Prepares the applications and paperwork that keep isotope and radiopharmaceutical facilities licensed and compliant with Health Canada and the CNSC.
careers.description: Regulatory affairs specialists prepare and manage submissions to Health Canada and the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC) needed to license, manufacture, and distribute isotopes and radiopharmaceuticals. They track changing regulations, coordinate cross-functional input for licence renewals and drug submissions, and help ensure ongoing compliance with regulatory commitments. Strong writing skills and a solid grasp of science and regulation are essential.
responsibilities: Prepare and submit licensing and compliance documents to the CNSC and Health Canada
Track regulatory changes affecting isotope and radiopharmaceutical operations
Coordinate input from quality, production, and safety teams for submissions
Maintain records supporting licence renewals and inspections
Respond to regulator information requests and deficiency letters
Advise internal teams on regulatory requirements for new products or processes
careers.dayToDay: A typical day involves drafting or reviewing sections of a regulatory submission, coordinating with technical teams to gather supporting data, and tracking deadlines for licence renewals or regulator responses.

careers.title: Medical Physicist / Internal Dosimetry Specialist
careers.summary: Calculates and models how much radiation dose a patient's organs and tumours actually receive from diagnostic and therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals, to keep treatments safe and effective.
careers.description: Medical physicists and internal dosimetry specialists apply physics to quantify and optimize radiation dose in nuclear medicine and radiopharmaceutical therapy, a field increasingly important as new theranostic drugs (paired diagnostic/therapeutic isotopes) reach patients. They build patient-specific dose models from imaging data, validate treatment protocols, and work alongside radiopharmacists, oncologists, and nuclear medicine physicians in hospitals, cancer centres, and research institutions.
responsibilities: Calculate patient-specific internal radiation doses from diagnostic and therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals
Develop and validate quantitative imaging and dosimetry protocols for theranostic procedures
Ensure radiation safety and regulatory compliance for nuclear medicine and radiotherapy programs
Collaborate with nuclear medicine physicians, radiopharmacists, and oncologists on treatment planning
Support clinical trials evaluating new radiopharmaceutical therapies
Maintain and calibrate imaging and dose-measurement equipment
careers.dayToDay: A typical day involves reviewing patient imaging scans to calculate organ and tumour dose, consulting with the clinical team on treatment plans, and validating equipment or software used for quantitative imaging.

careers.title: Research Scientist / Preclinical Scientist
careers.summary: Designs and tests new isotopes, targeting molecules, and imaging or therapy agents in the lab before they are studied in people.
careers.description: Preclinical research scientists develop and evaluate novel radioisotopes, targeting ligands, and radiopharmaceutical formulations, working from early discovery chemistry through in vitro and in vivo evaluation. They typically hold graduate training in chemistry, radiochemistry, or a related life science and work in university, government, or industry labs alongside radiochemists and clinical teams to help move new imaging and therapeutic agents toward human trials.
responsibilities: Design and synthesize new radiolabeled compounds and targeting molecules
Run preclinical evaluation studies of imaging and therapeutic radiopharmaceutical candidates
Analyze experimental data and prepare results for publication or regulatory submission
Collaborate with radiochemists, physicists, and clinical partners on translational research
Maintain laboratory safety and quality standards for work with radioactive materials
Contribute to grant applications and research funding proposals
careers.dayToDay: A typical day includes running experiments or radiosyntheses in the lab, analyzing data from prior studies, and meeting with collaborators to plan the next phase of a research project.
topEmployers: Centre for Probe Development and Commercialization (CPDC)

careers.title: Clinical Research Coordinator / Clinical Trial Specialist
careers.summary: Keeps radiopharmaceutical clinical trials running smoothly by coordinating patient visits, paperwork, and the safe handling of investigational doses.
careers.description: Clinical research coordinators manage the day-to-day operations of clinical trials involving new diagnostic or therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals, including patient scheduling, informed consent, data collection, and coordination of investigational product logistics with pharmacy and imaging teams. They work in hospitals, cancer centres, and contract research organizations, ensuring studies follow Health Canada and Good Clinical Practice requirements.
responsibilities: Coordinate patient recruitment, scheduling, and informed consent for clinical trials
Track and document investigational radiopharmaceutical product receipt, storage, and administration
Maintain accurate trial records and ensure compliance with Health Canada and GCP requirements
Liaise between investigators, sponsors, pharmacy, and imaging or treatment teams
Support data collection, adverse event reporting, and study audits
Coordinate logistics for time-sensitive investigational dose delivery
careers.dayToDay: A typical day includes checking in with trial participants, coordinating dose delivery and administration timing with pharmacy staff, and updating study records and regulatory documentation.

careers.title: Medical Science Liaison / Medical Affairs Specialist
careers.summary: Acts as the scientific bridge between a radiopharmaceutical company and the doctors and hospitals who use its products, sharing evidence and answering clinical questions.
careers.description: Medical science liaisons and medical affairs specialists communicate clinical and scientific evidence about diagnostic and therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals to physicians, treatment centres, and internal teams. They support product launches, respond to unsolicited medical inquiries, gather field insights on clinical practice, and help design or support investigator-initiated studies. The role typically requires an advanced science or health degree and strong communication skills.
responsibilities: Communicate clinical and scientific data on radiopharmaceutical products to healthcare providers
Respond to unsolicited medical and scientific inquiries from clinicians
Gather field insights on clinical practice and emerging treatment needs
Support investigator-initiated studies and continuing medical education
Collaborate with internal medical affairs, marketing, and regulatory teams
Represent the company at medical conferences and treatment centres
careers.dayToDay: A typical day involves meeting with nuclear medicine physicians or oncologists to discuss clinical data, preparing scientific materials, and coordinating with internal medical affairs colleagues on emerging questions from the field.

careers.title: Clinical Applications Specialist
careers.summary: Trains hospital staff and troubleshoots equipment and software so nuclear medicine and radiopharmaceutical technologies get used correctly and safely.
careers.description: Clinical applications specialists support the rollout and correct clinical use of nuclear medicine imaging equipment, dosimetry software, and radiopharmaceutical products in hospitals and clinics. They train technologists and physicians on new systems, troubleshoot technical issues, and act as a link between equipment manufacturers and clinical end users. Many come from a technologist, biomedical engineering technology, or applied science background.
responsibilities: Train clinical staff on new nuclear medicine equipment, software, or radiopharmaceutical products
Provide on-site and remote technical troubleshooting support
Support installation, calibration, and validation of imaging and dosimetry systems
Act as liaison between manufacturers, sales teams, and clinical end users
Document workflows and best practices for clinical adoption
Gather user feedback to inform product improvements
careers.dayToDay: A typical day includes visiting or remotely supporting a clinical site to train staff on equipment or software, resolving a technical issue, and coordinating with the vendor's product and sales teams.

careers.title: Sales / Account Manager / Business Development
careers.summary: Builds relationships with hospitals and clinics to help them adopt and purchase diagnostic and therapeutic radiopharmaceutical products.
careers.description: Sales and account managers in the radiopharmaceutical and medical isotope industry manage customer relationships with hospitals, imaging clinics, and healthcare systems, guiding the adoption of diagnostic and therapeutic products and negotiating supply agreements. They combine technical product knowledge with business development skills, often traveling within a territory to support customers and identify new partnership opportunities.
responsibilities: Manage relationships with hospital, clinic, and health authority customers
Promote and explain the clinical and technical benefits of radiopharmaceutical products
Negotiate supply agreements and pricing with healthcare purchasers
Identify and develop new business and partnership opportunities
Coordinate with clinical applications and logistics teams to support customer onboarding
Track sales targets and territory performance
careers.dayToDay: A typical day includes meeting with hospital purchasing or clinical staff, following up on orders or contracts, and coordinating with internal teams to resolve customer needs.

careers.title: Medical Courier / Radiopharmaceutical Logistics & Supply Chain
careers.summary: Moves time-sensitive radioactive doses safely and quickly from production sites to hospitals before they decay.
careers.description: Medical couriers and radiopharmaceutical logistics specialists manage the tightly time-constrained transport of radioactive isotopes and doses from cyclotrons, reactors, or radiopharmacies to hospitals and clinics. Because many isotopes decay within hours, this work demands precise scheduling, compliance with transport regulations for radioactive materials, and close coordination with production and clinical teams.
responsibilities: Transport radioactive doses and isotope products within strict time windows
Follow federal transport of dangerous goods regulations for radioactive materials
Coordinate delivery schedules with production sites, pharmacies, and hospitals
Maintain chain-of-custody documentation and radiation safety records
Respond to schedule changes caused by isotope decay timing or clinical needs
Inspect and maintain specialized transport containers and vehicles
careers.dayToDay: A typical day involves picking up freshly produced isotope doses, planning the fastest safe route to each delivery site, and completing documentation confirming safe, on-time delivery.

careers.title: Project / Program Manager
careers.summary: Plans and coordinates complex projects, such as new facility construction or product launches, across reactor, cyclotron, radiopharmacy, and healthcare teams.
careers.description: Project and program managers in the isotope and radiopharmaceutical sector coordinate cross-functional initiatives such as facility construction, equipment installation, new product implementation, and regulatory readiness projects. They manage timelines, budgets, and stakeholders across engineering, clinical, regulatory, and operations teams, often at reactor operators, cyclotron facilities, or radiopharmaceutical manufacturers.
responsibilities: Plan, budget, and schedule facility, equipment, or product-implementation projects
Coordinate cross-functional teams across engineering, clinical, and regulatory groups
Track project risks, timelines, and deliverables through completion
Report project status to leadership and external stakeholders
Manage vendor and contractor relationships for infrastructure projects
Support regulatory and safety readiness milestones for new facilities or programs
careers.dayToDay: A typical day includes running status meetings with project teams, updating schedules and budgets, and resolving issues that could delay a facility or product milestone.

institutions.name: Ontario Tech University
institutions.description: Public university offering Canada's only accredited undergraduate Nuclear Engineering program, an undergraduate Health Physics and Radiation Science program, and graduate nuclear engineering degrees.

institutions.name: McMaster University
institutions.description: Research university with a Department of Physics & Astronomy offering an Honours Physics program with a Medical and Biological Physics option, and home to the McMaster Nuclear Reactor.

institutions.name: Durham College
institutions.description: Public college offering applied-science and engineering-technology diplomas, including chemical engineering technology (with nuclear-physics content) and a non-destructive evaluation program, situated near Ontario's nuclear generating stations.

institutions.name: The Michener Institute of Education at UHN
institutions.description: Applied health-sciences college that delivers clinical medical-radiation-sciences education jointly with the University of Toronto, including the Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging Technology program.

institutions.name: University of Toronto
institutions.description: Research university whose Faculty of Applied Science and Engineering offers Engineering Science, an extremely competitive program with majors including Engineering Physics that feeds into nuclear engineering and health-physics careers.

institutions.name: Toronto Metropolitan University (TMU)
institutions.description: Public university whose Faculty of Science offers one of only five undergraduate Medical Physics programs in Canada, plus a CAMPEP-accredited graduate Medical Physics program.

institutions.name: University of Waterloo
institutions.description: Research university whose School of Pharmacy runs Canada's only co-op Doctor of Pharmacy (PharmD) program, with a direct-from-high-school Conditional Admission to Pharmacy (CAP) pathway via its Honours Science program.

institutions.name: University of British Columbia
institutions.description: UBC is a top research university and TRIUMF partner offering an Engineering Physics program with nuclear and particle physics pathways.

institutions.name: British Columbia Institute of Technology
institutions.description: BCIT is BC's leading polytechnic and the only institution in the province offering a Nuclear Medicine Technology diploma.

institutions.name: University of Alberta
institutions.description: The University of Alberta hosts a CAMPEP-accredited Medical Physics graduate program within its Department of Oncology.

institutions.name: Southern Alberta Institute of Technology
institutions.description: SAIT is Alberta's only institution offering an accredited Nuclear Medicine Technology diploma program.

institutions.name: University of Saskatchewan
institutions.description: A major research university whose College of Engineering and Department of Physics and Engineering Physics work alongside the Sylvia Fedoruk Canadian Centre for Nuclear Innovation and the province's cyclotron.

institutions.name: University of Manitoba
institutions.description: Manitoba's largest research university, whose Department of Physics and Astronomy offers a CAMPEP-track Medical Physics program delivered with CancerCare Manitoba.

institutions.name: University of New Brunswick
institutions.description: UNB's Faculty of Engineering offers a Nuclear Power specialization within Chemical Engineering, with deep ties to NB Power's Point Lepreau Nuclear Generating Station.

institutions.name: Dalhousie University
institutions.description: Dalhousie offers a CAMPEP-accredited Medical Physics graduate degree and an entry-to-practice Nuclear Medicine Technology degree through its School of Health Sciences.

institutions.name: Memorial University of Newfoundland
institutions.description: Memorial's Faculty of Science offers Physics and Chemistry degree programs that provide foundational training relevant to radiation science and radiochemistry careers.

educationPrograms.name: Bachelor of Engineering (Honours) in Nuclear Engineering
educationPrograms.description: Canada's only accredited undergraduate Nuclear Engineering program, covering the full nuclear fuel cycle, plant design, radiation protection, nuclear chemistry and materials, and reactor physics, with a direct-entry co-op option.
educationPrograms.requirements: OSSD with six 4U/4M credits including English (ENG4U, minimum 60%), Advanced Functions (MHF4U), Calculus and Vectors (MCV4U), Chemistry (SCH4U), and Physics (SPH4U); combined minimum 70% average across the prerequisite math and science courses, with no individual grade below 60%. Admission is competitive and the effective cutoff varies by year.

educationPrograms.name: Honours Physics (Medical and Biological Physics option available)
educationPrograms.description: McMaster's physics degree lets students pursue a Medical and Biological Physics concentration alongside general Honours Physics and Astrophysics, a common pathway toward health-physics and medical-physics careers.
educationPrograms.requirements: Ontario high school requirements: ENG4U, MCV4U, MHF4U, SCH4U, SPH4U. The Physics & Astronomy department lists an admission average in the low-to-high 80s depending on the specific first-year gateway chosen (e.g., life-sciences vs. math/physics entry); exact cutoffs vary by year and are not published as a single fixed number.

educationPrograms.name: Chemical Engineering Technology (Co-op option available)
educationPrograms.description: Ontario College Advanced Diploma covering analytical chemistry, organic chemistry, nuclear physics, and instrumental analysis; graduates work as chemical, nuclear-lab, and radio-chemical technologists, including a dedicated Nuclear Physics course in the final semester.
educationPrograms.duration: 6 semesters (3 years), plus optional 8-month co-op work terms
educationPrograms.requirements: Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD) or Mature Student Status, plus Grade 12 English (College or University level) and Grade 12 Mathematics (College, Mixed, or University level). Grade 12 Chemistry, Grade 12 Physics, and Technical Mathematics are recommended but not mandatory.

educationPrograms.name: Mechanical Engineering Technician — Non-Destructive Evaluation (fast-track)
educationPrograms.description: Ontario College Diploma covering liquid-penetrant, ultrasonic, magnetic-particle, eddy-current, and radiographic (including radiation-safety) testing methods, leading to NDT personnel certification eligibility under CGSB standard 48.9712.
educationPrograms.requirements: This is a second-entry, post-diploma program, not a direct-from-high-school program: applicants need an existing college diploma or university degree in engineering, industrial trades, or science, plus proof of English proficiency. Applicants whose prior credential is more than 10 years old may instead qualify with 3+ years of related industry experience plus specific post-secondary math and science coursework. There is no direct Ontario Grade 12 (4U) course-code pathway into this specific program.

educationPrograms.name: Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging Technology (University of Toronto Joint Program)
educationPrograms.description: Joint program between the University of Toronto and The Michener Institute leading to a Bachelor of Science in Medical Radiation Sciences plus an Advanced Diploma; includes radiopharmaceutical preparation, gamma-camera and SPECT/CT/PET-CT imaging, and 48 weeks of clinical placement.
educationPrograms.requirements: Second-entry program: applicants need a minimum of one year (10 single-semester courses) of university education with a CGPA of at least 2.70 (B-), including one single-semester university-level course in each of Biology, Mathematics, Physics, and Social Science, plus Grade 12 U-level Chemistry (SCH4U) or equivalent. Because entry requires a prior year of university rather than direct high-school admission, the underlying Ontario high-school preparation (typically SBI4U, SCH4U, SPH4U, and MHF4U/MCV4U to gain that university admission in the first place) is an inference, not a directly stated program requirement.

educationPrograms.name: Engineering Science (Engineering Physics and other majors)
educationPrograms.description: One of Canada's most competitive engineering programs, entering all students into a shared first two years before they choose a major in third year, including Engineering Physics and Energy Systems Engineering, both relevant to nuclear-engineer and health-physicist career paths.
educationPrograms.requirements: All applicants to U of T Engineering (including Engineering Science) must complete senior-level Advanced Functions (MHF4U), Calculus & Vectors (MCV4U), Chemistry (SCH4U), and Physics (SPH4U), plus English (ENG4U) and one additional 4U/M course. Admission is extremely competitive: reported competitive averages for Engineering Science are in the mid-to-high 90s, though U of T does not publish a single official minimum cutoff, as the effective bar varies year to year with applicant volume.

educationPrograms.name: Medical Physics - BSc (Hons)
educationPrograms.description: One of only 5 undergraduate Medical Physics programs in Canada, covering medical imaging, radiation therapy, radiation protection, and health physics, with an optional 5-year co-op. Career possibilities listed by TMU include clinical medical physicist and radiation therapist.
educationPrograms.requirements: OSSD with completion of 6 Grade 12 U or M courses and a minimum overall average of 70%, including required Grade 12 U courses (minimum grade of 65% in each): English (ENG4U/EAE4U preferred), Advanced Functions (MHF4U), and 2 of Physics (SPH4U), Chemistry (SCH4U), or Biology (SBI4U). TMU notes the average needed for admission fluctuates year to year; recent grade ranges have been in the mid-70s.

educationPrograms.name: Honours Science (Conditional Admission to Pharmacy pathway)
educationPrograms.description: Waterloo's Honours Science program offers outstanding high school students pre-admission to Waterloo's Doctor of Pharmacy (PharmD) program -- Canada's only co-op PharmD -- through Conditional Admission to Pharmacy (CAP) status, a direct pathway toward radiopharmacist and other pharmacy careers.
educationPrograms.duration: 4 years (Honours Science) leading into the 4-year PharmD
educationPrograms.requirements: A final grade of at least 70% is required in English (ENG4U), Advanced Functions (MHF4U), and Calculus and Vectors (MCV4U), plus any 2 of Biology (SBI4U), Chemistry (SCH4U), Earth and Space Science (SES4U), Data Management (MDM4U), or Physics (SPH4U), and one additional 4U/M course. SBI4U, SCH4U, SES4U, and SPH4U are all recommended even though only 2 of them are formally required.

educationPrograms.name: Bachelor of Science (Honours) in Health Physics and Radiation Science
educationPrograms.description: One of a limited number of Health Physics and Radiation Science programs in Canada, run by Ontario Tech's Department of Energy and Nuclear Engineering, covering radiation detection and measurement, medical imaging, radiation biophysics/dosimetry, and industrial and therapeutic applications of radiation, with two thesis projects in the final year.
educationPrograms.requirements: Ontario Tech's own program page for Health Physics and Radiation Science did not display a distinct admission-requirements table when checked; the figures here are inferred from the identical admission-requirement template published for Ontario Tech's sibling Physics-family programs (Physics, Astrophysics, Nanophysics), which are run by the same Faculty and explicitly cross-promote the Health Physics and Radiation Science program: OSSD with six 4U/4M credits including English (ENG4U), Advanced Functions (MHF4U), and two of Biology (SBI4U), Calculus and Vectors (MCV4U), Chemistry (SCH4U), or Physics (SPH4U); combined minimum 70% average in prerequisite math and science courses. This should be verified directly with Ontario Tech admissions before publishing to end users.

educationPrograms.name: Engineering Physics (BASc)
educationPrograms.description: A five-year Bachelor of Applied Science program combining core engineering training with a strong foundation in physics and mathematics. Students select technical electives that allow specialization in areas such as nuclear/particle instrumentation, materials, or electrical systems, with proximity to TRIUMF research opportunities.
educationPrograms.requirements: Completion of first-year Applied Science (Engineering) at UBC, including BC Grade 12 English, Pre-Calculus 12, Chemistry 12, and Physics 12 (or equivalents), followed by a competitive second-year application including an interview for entry into Engineering Physics.

educationPrograms.name: Nuclear Medicine Diploma
educationPrograms.description: A two-year full-time diploma preparing students to become Registered Technologists in Nuclear Medicine (RTNM). The program combines on-campus instruction with in-hospital clinical rotations covering radiopharmaceutical administration, diagnostic imaging, and radiation safety, leading to CAMRT certification eligibility.
educationPrograms.requirements: Minimum 73% (or equivalent) in English Studies 12, Pre-Calculus 12, Chemistry 12, Physics 11, and a Grade 12-level Anatomy and Physiology/Biology course, plus completion of a medical terminology course, CPR certification, and a criminal record check.

educationPrograms.name: Medical Physics (MSc)
educationPrograms.description: A CAMPEP-accredited, research-based Master of Science program in the Department of Oncology focused on the application of ionizing radiation for cancer diagnosis and treatment. Students complete required coursework in radiation physics and dosimetry alongside a thesis in areas such as radiotherapy, PET imaging, or Monte Carlo dose calculations.
educationPrograms.duration: up to 4 years (typically 2 years coursework plus thesis)
educationPrograms.requirements: A Bachelor's degree in Physics, Engineering Physics, or a closely related discipline with a minimum GPA of 2.7 (B+ average recommended over the last two years); undergraduate preparation should include Physics, Mathematics, and Chemistry coursework.

educationPrograms.name: Nuclear Medicine Technology Diploma
educationPrograms.description: A two-and-a-half-year diploma preparing students for careers as nuclear medicine technologists, covering radiobiology, radiation safety, diagnostic imaging, CT, and patient care through classroom instruction and clinical practicum placements in hospitals and clinics.
educationPrograms.requirements: Combined average of 75% including Math 30-1 (70%) or Math 30-2 (75%), English Language Arts 30-1 (70%), Chemistry 30 (70%), and one of Biology 30, Physics 30, or Math 31 (70%), plus passing the School of Health and Public Safety's entrance testing process.

educationPrograms.name: Engineering Physics (B.E.)
educationPrograms.description: A CEAB-accredited engineering degree bridging fundamental physics and applied engineering, covering topics such as instrumentation, materials, and advanced technology systems. Students complete a common first-year core before entering the upper-year Engineering Physics stream, with opportunities to connect to nuclear-related research through campus facilities like the Fedoruk Centre and the Saskatchewan cyclotron.
educationPrograms.requirements: Direct entry from high school requiring roughly 70% or better in Grade 12 Physics, Chemistry, Pre-Calculus, and English (Saskatchewan curriculum), or equivalent for out-of-province applicants.

educationPrograms.name: Physics and Engineering Physics (M.Sc./Ph.D.)
educationPrograms.description: Graduate research program in the Department of Physics and Engineering Physics offering thesis-based study in experimental and theoretical fields, including nuclear, particle, and medical physics research connected to the Sylvia Fedoruk Canadian Centre for Nuclear Innovation and the Saskatchewan Centre for Cyclotron Sciences.
educationPrograms.requirements: An Honours B.Sc. (or equivalent) in physics, engineering physics, or a related field; admission also requires meeting College of Graduate and Postdoctoral Studies English-proficiency and academic standards.

educationPrograms.name: Physics and Astronomy, M.Sc. — Comprehensive Medical Physics
educationPrograms.description: A course-based, CAMPEP-oriented M.Sc. specialization delivered with CancerCare Manitoba, covering radiation protection, medical radiation physics, radiation therapy physics, diagnostic imaging (MRI, ultrasound, X-ray), and nuclear medicine physics. Replaces a thesis with an 18-month coursework sequence plus a 6-month clinical research project and closing oral examination.
educationPrograms.requirements: An Honours B.Sc. in Physics and Astronomy, Mathematics and Physics, Engineering Physics, or an equivalent degree; applicants without this background may need pre-Master's coursework, and all applicants must meet Faculty of Graduate Studies admission and English-proficiency standards.

educationPrograms.name: Bachelor of Science in Engineering, Chemical Engineering (Nuclear Power Specialization)
educationPrograms.description: A Chemical Engineering degree with an optional Nuclear Power specialization, offered once students complete 80 credit hours, covering nuclear engineering fundamentals, nuclear chemical processes, corrosion, nuclear reactor physics, and nuclear safety and reliability. Draws on UNB's long-standing relationship with NB Power and the Point Lepreau Nuclear Generating Station.
educationPrograms.requirements: Grade 12 English, Advanced Functions/Trigonometry, Calculus, Chemistry, and Physics, each typically at 70%+, with a competitive overall admission average (around 75%+) required for entry into Engineering.

educationPrograms.name: Medical Physics (MSc)
educationPrograms.description: A CAMPEP-accredited, thesis-based master's degree combining coursework and hands-on research in imaging and radiation oncology medical physics, delivered through the Department of Physics and Atmospheric Science in partnership with hospital treatment and imaging facilities. Graduates are eligible to enter residency training programs in medical physics.
educationPrograms.requirements: An undergraduate degree in Physics or a closely related field with strong standing, meeting Dalhousie Faculty of Graduate Studies admission requirements plus program-specific prerequisites in physics and mathematics.

educationPrograms.name: Health Sciences (Nuclear Medicine Technology) (BHSc)
educationPrograms.description: An entry-to-practice bachelor's degree preparing students to become certified nuclear medicine technologists who administer radiopharmaceuticals for diagnostic and therapeutic imaging. Combines academic coursework with clinical practicums across Atlantic Canada and leads to CAMRT certification eligibility.
educationPrograms.requirements: Minimum overall average of 75%, with Grade 12 English, Mathematics, Physics, and Chemistry each at 70% or higher, plus one additional academic subject; reserved seats are available for residents of NB, PE, and NL.

educationPrograms.name: Bachelor of Science (Physics)
educationPrograms.description: A general BSc program covering Newtonian mechanics, electricity and magnetism, thermodynamics, and quantum mechanics, with opportunities for experimental, theoretical, and computational work. Physics cannot be declared as a major until after first-year coursework, following Memorial's direct-entry Faculty of Science admission model.
educationPrograms.requirements: High school graduation with senior-level Mathematics and laboratory science (Physics and/or Chemistry recommended) among required credits, plus general Memorial University admission standards; declaring Physics as a major requires 30 credit hours including math and physics coursework.

educationPrograms.name: Chemistry Major (BSc)
educationPrograms.description: A Canadian Society for Chemistry-accredited general degree covering general and analytical chemistry, organic chemistry, physical chemistry, and biochemistry, with required supporting coursework in physics and mathematics. Provides a foundation for careers involving chemical analysis, quality control, and radiochemical work.
educationPrograms.requirements: High school graduation meeting Memorial's general Faculty of Science admission standards, including senior Mathematics and laboratory science; declaring a Chemistry major requires foundational university-level chemistry, physics, and math coursework.

companies.name: Centre for Probe Development and Commercialization (CPDC)
